newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean President Kim's reform plans in jeopardy.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean President Kim's reform plans in jeopardy.

text.p: A ruling party request to delay financial reform legislation could prevent South Korean President Kim Young-sam from achieving meaningful economic reform before his term ends, economists said on Thursday.

The ruling New Korea Party has asked the government to postpone introduction of legislation which would usher in financial reforms being drawn up by a presidential commission, a party official said on Thursday.
The party believes the government needs more time to consider the proposals, he said.

Late on Thursday, Finance Minister Kang Kyong-shik told reporters he would try to implement financial reforms by submitting reform legislation to parliament by September at the latest. He gave no further details.
But a finance ministry official said: "It looks impossible as the country would be caught in an election mood from July."
He said lawmakers, concerned about votes, were unlikely to take up contentious issues so near the mid-December presidential vote.
The reforms include such key issues as central bank independence, business conglomerate participation in bank management and mergers of financial institutions.

"(The ruling party's request) takes everything back to square one," said Lee In-hyung, research director at LG Economic Research Institute. "It's unlikely the government would implement financial reform this year.

"We shouldn't have expected too much from the lame-duck President," said Lee Hahn-koo, president of Daewoo Economic Research Institute. "If he really wanted a series of reforms, he should have pushed forward from the beginning, when he first took power."
Kim's term expires next February. He is barred from seeking a second term.

Kim, who assumed office in 1993, was elected on promises of reforms. He has said sweeping anti-graft and social reforms were "painful surgery to remove a malignant tumour" and could not be stopped. But he has been unable to follow through on his promises.
He backed away from a controversial labour law rammed through parliament last December after workers responded with some of South Korea's worst protests and strikes in years.
The original law would have allowed employers greater latitude to lay off workers, a provision seen as crucial if troubled firms were to be encouraged to restructure.
In January, Kim agreed to a watered-down version that would delay implementation of the clause on lay-offs for two years.
"The government has back-pedalled on deregulation," said Rhee Namuh, head of research at Dongbang Peregrine.
"The new labour law was the signal that the government had retreated from reform. This means it will not strongly support any kind of reforms," he said.

President Kim set up the 31-member Presidential Commission for Financial Reform in January. He said its goal was to prevent another scandal involving banks and politicians similar to that surrounding Hanbo Steel Co.
That scandal, which has spread to the president's family and a number of business groups, is still being probed.
The presidential panel was to report its mid-term financial reform proposals to President Kim by the end of this month.
The ruling party official quoted Kim Zoong-wie, chairman of the party's policy committee, as saying the proposals contained "controversial issues".

For example, the panel was working on a plan to exclude the Finance Ministry from the central bank's operations, analysts said. The commission proposed that the central bank governor chair the Monetary Board, which decides monetary policies. The finance minister heads the board and has the right to recommend to the president five of nine board members.
